newsitem.title: INDIA: Will El Nino hurt India's monsoon? Too soon to say.
newsitem.headline: Will El Nino hurt India's monsoon? Too soon to say.

text.p: El Nino warm water currents could threaten crucial monsoon rains in India but it is too early to predict their impact on crop production, meteorological officials and analysts said on Wednesday.

Oil World reported on Tuesday that the development of El Nino in the southern Pacific had increased the chance of drought across southeast Asia, Australia and India, threatening oilseeds and grain crops.
"Due to El Nino, monsoon rains in India could be weaker and more erratic than usual," the Hamburg-based newsletter said.

El Nino raises the temperature of water off the coast of South America and can disrupt normal weather patterns worldwide. The last severe El Nino took place in 1983 and caused billions of dollars in damage to crops around the world.

Meteorological experts said it was too early to determine how El Nino would affect India's annual southwestern monsoon rains, which broke over the southern and northeastern regions of the subcontinent on Monday, 10 days later than usual.
"It is too early to predict the impact," R.R. Kelkar, a senior official with the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD), told Reuters.
He said an update on the progress of El Nino and its impact on monsoon rains could be possible only by the end of June.

Last month, the IMD predicted a "normal" monsoon for the 10th consecutive year. Nine of 16 measures the department monitors to predict the monsoon indicated rainfall would be about 92 percent of the long-term average.
But the IMD also said the El Nino pattern, which had been near normal since 1995, was exhibiting an "unfavourable trend" this year.
The department said El Nino's parametres needed "to be carefully monitored in view of their likely adverse impact on the monsoon rainfall".

S.M. Virmani of Hyderabad-based International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Crops said the exact impact of El Nino, which is one of the 16 measures used in IMD's model, could not currently be quantified.
"But as per indications, certainly it is likely to have a negative impact this time," Virmani told Reuters by telephone.

Virmani said each day's delay in the arrival of the monsoon meant the loss of about 0.25 percent of India's crop production. As the rains this year broke 10 days late, the crop loss can currently be forecast at about 2.5 percent, he said.
The monsoon rains usually start around June 1 and move progressively north, eventually covering the country before tapering off in September.
"The delay in monsoon will have a slight impact on crops but the overall impact depends on how the monsoon progresses over time," a senior Agriculture Ministry official told Reuters.
During the four months of the southwest monsoon season, India receives an average of about 88 cm of rain, which amounts to 80 percent of annual rainfall.
The monsoon rains are crucial to agriculture and the broader economy. Agriculture employs about two thirds of India's workers and accounts for more than a quarter of its gross domestic product.
Adequate rainfall can bolster farm production, add to national income and keep prices down.
